impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive rights to a licensee but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that the patent owner retained a non-illusory right to exclude others from practicing the patented invention, which satisfies the irreducible constitutional minimum of standing. This clarifies that patentees can structure licensing agreements to grant exclusive commercial rights while preserving litigation standing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring licensing deals can retain meaningful litigation rights by carefully drafting agreements that preserve the right to sue for infringement, enabling them to monetize patents through licensing while maintaining enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face greater exposure as patent holders with exclusive licensees can independently pursue infringement suits, even where substantial commercial rights have been licensed away.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's anti-CGRP antibody patent claims were invalid for lack of written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112, after a jury found the claims valid and willfully infringed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating the jury's findings that Teva's headache treatment patents covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were valid and willfully infringed by Lilly. This is a significant ruling in the high-stakes CGRP migraine treatment market involving Teva's Ajovy product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies benefit from a more protective standard for written description and enablement of antibody claims, supporting broader patent protection for biologic drug classes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar developers face potentially broader blocking patents on therapeutic antibody classes, which may delay market entry and increase licensing costs.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instructions and verdict form regarding patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and whether a single infringement question covering all asserted patents in a verdict form requires a new trial.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's use of a single infringement question covering multiple patents was prejudicial error. The court also vacated the § 101 eligibility determination for the '495 patent under Alice step two while affirming eligibility for other patents. This decision impacts how patent trials are structured when multiple patents are asserted.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement of separate infringement findings for each patent, preventing generalized verdicts that obscure which patents were actually infringed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face increased procedural complexity and risk of vacated verdicts if verdict forms do not separately address each patent's infringement.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar invalidity grounds that were not raised in a prior IPR petition, based on whether a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered the prior art.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's estoppel ruling, finding insufficient evidence to support estopping one invalidity ground and failure to account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous analysis of what a skilled searcher could have reasonably discovered before barring invalidity defenses in district court.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers retain broader ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court litigation, as courts must more carefully assess whether prior art was reasonably discoverable before applying IPR estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face diminished benefit from the IPR estoppel provision, as defendants may more easily argue that prior art grounds were not reasonably discoverable and thus not estopped.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove its asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, reasoning that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The permanent injunction and exemplary damages were vacated.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from a rigorous evidentiary standard requiring plaintiffs to demonstrate that asserted trade secrets are not generally known in the industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure they can clearly demonstrate the novelty and secrecy of their claimed trade secrets, as generally known information will not qualify for protection even if kept confidential internally.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit, where Insulet allegedly knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and JMOL denial, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred as a matter of law. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of EOFlow's alleged misappropriation of its insulin patch pump trade secrets more than three years before filing suit, triggering the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing certainty and finality against stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation, as delays beyond three years will bar DTSA claims regardless of the merits, potentially forfeiting substantial damages.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding a trade secret damages expert's testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the breach of contract jury award, reinstating the original verdict. This case significantly impacts how damages are measured in software trade secret cases involving complex enterprise software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from broader acceptance of damages models in trade secret cases and the reinstatement of jury contract damages awards, strengthening enforcement of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Licensees like Ford face exposure to larger damages awards in trade secret and breach of contract cases, particularly where they develop competing products during a licensing relationship.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted farming data collection patent claims were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional. The decision reinforces that claims directed to data collection, processing, and sharing using conventional technology remain vulnerable to § 101 challenges in the agricultural technology space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing agricultural data patents benefit from continued strong application of § 101 to invalidate claims directed to abstract data processing concepts, and may recover fees on remand.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech companies seeking patent protection for data-driven farming solutions face significant § 101 eligibility hurdles, limiting their ability to protect innovations built on data collection and analysis.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages analysis and infringement findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated the district court's summary judgment of patent eligibility, finding that certain claims of two patents required further analysis under Alice, while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents. The court also affirmed the infringement and damages findings, including the denial of motions to exclude damages expert testimony. This case provides important guidance on § 101 eligibility for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain technical constellation design claims, supporting patent protection for improvements to digital communication standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued exposure to patent infringement claims on communications technology, with the court affirming broad damages theories.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory for multicore processor patents, and whether striking damages expert theories was appropriate.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine issues of material fact on VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, while affirming on other grounds. The case addresses important questions about extraterritorial application of patent law to semiconductor manufacturing and the scope of DOE in complex processor architecture cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent assertion entities and patent holders benefit from the court's recognition that doctrine of equivalents theories can survive summary judgment in complex semiconductor cases, preserving paths to infringement findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor manufacturers face continued uncertainty regarding infringement liability for global manufacturing processes, as DOE theories may be difficult to resolve at summary judgment.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that sales expressly disclose the prior art device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and rejecting the argument that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of a device's functionality. This clarifies evidentiary standards for prior art sales challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from broader admissibility of corporate representative testimony in invalidity challenges, making it easier to establish the on-sale bar using historical corporate knowledge.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar invalidation, as prior commercial sales need not expressly disclose the patented functionality to trigger the bar.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline for seeking a stay in a previously filed action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that BioMarin could not obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled declaratory judgment action by dismissing and refiling its own action after missing the 30-day deadline under § 1659(a)(2). This prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court proceedings involving pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies seeking declaratory judgments of non-infringement benefit from protection against tactical delay by ITC complainants who attempt to restart statutory deadlines by refiling actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC complainants who miss the 30-day stay deadline cannot cure the deficiency through procedural maneuvering, potentially losing the ability to delay parallel district court proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that the pH limitation must be measured at the standard temperature recognized in the field and that Actelion was barred from and failed to prove doctrine of equivalents infringement. This is significant for Hatch-Waxman ANDA litigation involving generic drug entry for hypertension treatments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from narrow claim construction of measurable parameters in formulation patents, facilitating generic market entry for important cardiovascular drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection when claims include measurable parameters, as courts will construe such terms according to standard measurement conditions in the field.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of sensor-based logistics patent claims, and whether a non-party to district court litigation can file an IPR petition on behalf of or in coordination with a litigation party to circumvent the § 315(b) time bar.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness finding and remanded, while declining to review the challenge to the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant concerns about potential abuse of the IPR system through coordinated filings by third parties to circumvent statutory time bars, impacting patent enforcement strategies for logistics and tracking technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the vacatur of the Board's obviousness determination, and the case highlights concerns about third-party IPR petitions that may lead to future restrictions on coordinated filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using the IPR system face uncertainty about the viability of coordinated filings where a non-party files on behalf of a time-barred litigation party.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage after most claims were invalidated in IPR, and whether attorneys' fees and sanctions were warranted under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the patent infringement complaint for surviving claims on the same obviousness grounds that invalidated the other claims in IPR, but reversed the exceptional case fee award under § 285 and the attorney sanction under § 1927, finding insufficient grounds for either. This provides important guidance on the limits of fee-shifting and attorney sanctions in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent litigators benefit from the reversal of fee-shifting and sanctions, as the court found that filing suit on surviving IPR claims, even if ultimately unsuccessful, does not automatically constitute exceptional conduct warranting fees.
impacts.negativeImplications: Defendants who prevail on validity grounds may face difficulty recovering fees and sanctions when plaintiffs assert claims that survived IPR, even if those claims are ultimately found invalid on the same grounds.
